w:r.w:t: MINISTRY OF HIGHER AND TERTIARY EDUCATION, INNOVATION,
Offline AI-Powered Precision Crop Disease Diagnostic System
Andile Prince Bhebhe and Edith Nqobile Muyambiri
Liquid Intelligent Technologies, Bulawayo; Omnishi AI; Harare Institute of Technology; ZB Innovation Hub, Harare
Agriculture, Food Security and Environmental Innovation

Crop diseases, particularly Northern Corn Leaf Blight (NCLB), cost Zimbabwe's 1.4 million smallholder maize farmers yield losses of 30 to 50 percent when infection establishes early in the season. Extension officers are overstretched, internet connectivity is absent across most rural areas, and existing digital advisory tools require cloud infrastructure that smallholder farmers do not have.

This system delivers offline, on-device AI-powered crop disease diagnosis. A convolutional neural network built on a lightweight MobileNetV3-Small backbone, fine-tuned on 1,821 field-collected maize-leaf photographs, runs inference entirely on the device with no internet required. A farmer photographs an affected leaf and receives an instant diagnosis in English, Shona or Ndebele with actionable treatment guidance. The model achieves 96.0 percent test accuracy and 0.960 macro-F1.

The same AI engine scales across four hardware tiers matched to farm size. Tier 1 (under 2 ha, smallholder): smartphone app requiring no SIM card or Wi-Fi. Tier 2 (2 to 20 ha): drone-mounted camera for aerial scouting and disease hotspot mapping, enabling targeted rather than blanket treatment. Tier 3 (20 to 200 ha): autonomous robotic ground vehicle for row-by-row canopy inspection with GPS geo-tagging. Tier 4 (above 200 ha, large commercial): module embedded directly in moving pivot or linear irrigation systems, diagnosing disease continuously as the arm sweeps across the field and issuing alerts before the next irrigation cycle.

The system advances SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) and SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure), responds directly to the inaugural Zimbabwe AI Grand Challenge (food security theme), and aligns with Zimbabwe's National AI Strategy 2026 to 2030.

This is the first documented offline, on-device AI diagnostic tool for maize disease tailored to Zimbabwean smallholder conditions. Key novelties include: (1) offline-first architecture with zero network dependency; (2) leakage-free, group-aware evaluation keeping all images from the same physical leaf in one partition, preventing inflated scores common in published plant-disease studies; (3) a four-tier hardware platform scaling from a handset to pivot-irrigation integration; and (4) multilingual output in English, Shona and Ndebele.

A fully functional prototype has been built and peer-reviewed. Dataset: 1,821 field-collected maize-leaf images with group-aware train/val/test split (1,299 / 273 / 249). Model: MobileNetV3-Small fine-tuned in PyTorch with class-weighted cross-entropy, AdamW optimiser and early stopping. Results: 96.0 percent test accuracy, 0.959 balanced accuracy, 0.960 macro-F1. Quantised to 8-bit integers, the model is a few megabytes and runs on a low-cost Android smartphone CPU. The paper has been submitted to JRISS Vol. 6, Issue 1, 2026.

The system closes the connectivity gap, replacing the absent extension officer for routine screening. Early NCLB detection enables timely intervention before the 30 to 50 percent yield loss threshold. Grad-CAM heat-maps confirm predictions rest on lesion tissue, making the AI reasoning visible and auditable by agronomists and farmers alike.

Tier 1 (smartphone): ready for pilot deployment today. Tier 2 (drone): aerial scouting over small farms, disease hotspot maps for precision spraying. Tier 3 (robotic ground vehicle): autonomous row-by-row inspection with geo-tagged outbreak maps. Tier 4 (pivot/linear irrigation): AI module on the irrigation arm diagnoses in motion across 200-plus-hectare estates, with treatment alerts delivered before the next irrigation pass. The model is hardware-agnostic and exportable to ONNX format for any edge device.

Precision diagnosis enables targeted fungicide application, reducing chemical inputs by treating only affected zones. This lowers pesticide runoff, soil contamination and imported agrochemical spend. The drone and robot tiers use electric drive with no direct emissions. Early detection reduces crop failure, lowering pressure to expand farmland into ecologically sensitive areas.

Zimbabwe's National AI Strategy 2026 to 2030 names agriculture as a priority sector and explicitly commits to AI for crop disease prevention, food security and smallholder support. The inaugural Zimbabwe AI Grand Challenge 2026 is dedicated to food security, the exact domain of this prototype. The system also advances NDS2 pillars on food security and digital transformation, and contributes to SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) and SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure).

The AI engine is trained once and deployed at near-zero marginal cost per diagnosis. Revenue streams include app subscriptions, institutional licensing to agri-input companies and NGOs, hardware bundles for Tiers 2 to 4, data analytics sales and SADC export licensing. Break-even is projected in Year 2.

Zimbabwe AI Grand Challenge provides immediate high-profile validation. Expressions of interest are being secured from agricultural input suppliers, development-finance institutions and farmer cooperative unions. The peer-reviewed JRISS paper provides the diagnostic accuracy evidence underpinning market confidence.

Direct roles include AI/ML engineers, software developers, field data collectors, agricultural domain experts, hardware integration technicians and sales support agents. Phase 1 targets 11 to 20 direct jobs; Phase 3 targets 21 or more. Indirect employment includes drone pilots, robot maintenance technicians and agronomist extension partners.

The tool reaches Zimbabwe's most marginalised agricultural households: subsistence farmers with no internet, no nearby extension officer and no financial buffer against crop loss. Multilingual support (English, Shona, Ndebele) and a one-button photo interface lower barriers for women farmers who head a majority of smallholder households in rural Zimbabwe.

Reduced NCLB losses lower the national maize import requirement, saving foreign exchange. Precision fungicide use cuts agrochemical imports. SADC licensing generates forex inflows from Year 2. Data analytics services sold to commodity traders and crop insurers provide additional hard-currency revenue.

Revenue streams: (1) freemium app -- USD 2/month per farmer, USD 15/year per cooperative group; (2) institutional licensing -- USD 0.50 to 1.00 per farmer reached annually; (3) hardware bundles for drone, robot and irrigation tiers; (4) data analytics sold to commodity traders and insurers; (5) SADC export licensing from Year 2. Projected revenues: USD 20,000 (Year 1), USD 118,000 (Year 2), USD 320,000 (Year 3). Net surplus: USD 48,000 (Year 2), USD 210,000 (Year 3). Foreign currency generation through SADC licensing and data service exports.
Estimated 18 to 24 months from first commercial deployment. The core AI asset is already built; remaining investment covers app hardening, go-to-market and hardware integration.

Year 1 -- Revenue USD 20,000 / Costs USD 45,000 / Deficit (USD 25,000). Year 2 -- Revenue USD 118,000 / Costs USD 70,000 / Surplus USD 48,000. Year 3 -- Revenue USD 320,000 / Costs USD 110,000 / Surplus USD 210,000. Projections are conservative and assume no grant funding beyond the initial PIA award.

Key risks and mitigations: (1) Model accuracy on new field conditions -- mitigated by independent cross-field validation and low-confidence deferral to extension officers. (2) Farmer digital literacy -- mitigated by one-button UI and partner onboarding via AGRITEX. (3) Drone/robot regulatory uncertainty -- mitigated by early CAAZ engagement with Phase 2 timeline absorbing lead time. (4) Agrochemical guidance liability -- mitigated by agronomist review and ZAMA product-list alignment.

Phase 1 (0 to 6 months): USD 40,000 for app hardening and pilot deployment in two districts. Phase 2 (6 to 18 months): USD 80,000 for multi-disease model, drone and robot integration, and independent test-set collection. Phase 3 (18 to 36 months): USD 150,000 for irrigation-system integration, treatment knowledge base and regional market entry. Total 3-year requirement: USD 270,000 -- grant, impact-investment or blended-finance eligible.

Target customers: Zimbabwe's 1.4 million smallholder maize households (Tier 1); commercial farmers, agribusinesses and cooperative unions (Tiers 2 to 4); government extension services (AGRITEX). The SADC digital agri-advisory market is estimated at USD 50 million and growing. Tier 1 is pilot-ready with no additional infrastructure required. Institutional demand confirmed through the Zimbabwe AI Grand Challenge and NAS 2026 to 2030 mandate.

Technology readiness levels by tier: Tier 1 smartphone -- TRL 6, pilot-deployable now. Tier 2 drone -- TRL 4, hardware integration design complete. Tier 3 robotic vehicle -- TRL 3, mechanical prototype in design. Tier 4 irrigation integration -- TRL 3, concept validated with pivot-irrigation partners. The AI model is exported in ONNX format and runs on ARM smartphone CPUs, drone companion computers and irrigation PLCs without modification.

Five revenue streams: (1) B2C freemium app scalable to 100,000-plus users across SADC at near-zero marginal cost per user; (2) B2B institutional licensing to input companies (Syngenta, Windmill), cooperatives and development NGOs; (3) B2G government procurement for national disease surveillance; (4) Hardware-as-a-Service drone and robot kits leased on a per-hectare-scouted fee; (5) Data-as-a-Service disease-incidence intelligence sold to commodity traders, insurers and agricultural lenders.

Mobile app: compliant with Zimbabwe's Data Protection Act 2021; no personal data collected beyond anonymised usage analytics. Drone operations: Civil Aviation Authority of Zimbabwe Part 101 compliance; operator licensing and no-fly-zone adherence required for Tier 2; engagement initiated. Agrochemical guidance: treatment recommendations reviewed by registered agronomists and aligned with ZAMA approved product lists. AI ethics: low-confidence cases deferred to human extension officers; consistent with NAS 2026 to 2030 responsible-AI principles.

The prototype has been developed with institutional support from Liquid Intelligent Technologies, Harare Institute of Technology and ZB Innovation Hub. The PIA award would provide catalytic funding and national profile to attract impact investors. Break-even in Year 2 and USD 210,000 surplus in Year 3 demonstrate strong return on catalytic investment. The combination of commercial revenue and measurable SDG impact meets the investment criteria of IFC, AfDB AgriTech windows and Zimbabwean impact funds.
